title: Science & Society: Truth Under Pressure
description: Navigate real-world scenarios where scientific thinking meets social pressure. Do you follow evidence — or what's comfortable?
coaching_moment: Scientific literacy is a soft skill. The ability to distinguish evidence from noise, and to update beliefs when facts change, is one of the most valuable traits in any professional.

rounds.title: Vaccine Debate
rounds.scenario: A parent asks you whether they should vaccinate their child. They've read social media posts claiming vaccines cause harm. What do you say?

choices.label: Share the scientific consensus and how to evaluate sources
choices.outcome: The parent appreciates the framework. They make an informed choice.

choices.label: Avoid conflict — say it's their choice and walk away
choices.outcome: You preserved the relationship but missed a chance to share life-saving information.

choices.label: Dismiss their concern as misinformation and lecture them
choices.outcome: They feel judged and disengage. The misinformation remains.

rounds.coaching_moment: Sharing evidence effectively requires empathy, not just facts. How you say it matters as much as what you say.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Climate Data
rounds.scenario: Your company's data shows your product contributes to carbon emissions. The data is valid. Leadership wants to bury it. What do you do?

choices.label: Report it internally and request a sustainability review
choices.outcome: Integrity preserved. You trigger a 6-month review. Long-term credibility gained.

choices.label: Comply with leadership — it's their call, not yours
choices.outcome: Short-term safety. Long-term: when the data leaks, you're implicated.

choices.label: Anonymously leak to a journalist
choices.outcome: Data goes public. Your company faces scrutiny. Your identity is eventually discovered.

rounds.coaching_moment: Whistleblowing vs. internal advocacy is a spectrum. Most ethical issues are best resolved by speaking up internally before escalating externally.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: AI Bias
rounds.scenario: An AI hiring tool your company uses consistently scores women 15% lower for technical roles. You discovered this. What do you do?

choices.label: Document the finding and escalate to the data team and legal
choices.outcome: The system is audited and fixed. You are recognized for catching a major liability.

choices.label: Manually override scores for female candidates without disclosure
choices.outcome: Fixes individual cases but the systemic issue persists. You've created an undocumented process.

choices.label: Stop using the tool for technical roles unilaterally
choices.outcome: Inconsistent policy. Some candidates benefit, others don't. Not scalable.

rounds.coaching_moment: Algorithmic bias is a systemic problem requiring systemic solutions. Individual overrides are not the fix.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Drug Trial Results
rounds.scenario: A clinical trial you helped run showed mixed results. The drug works for some populations but not others. Your company wants to publish only the positive subgroup.

choices.label: Insist all results be published — selective reporting is research fraud
choices.outcome: Full results published. The drug is approved only for appropriate populations. Science wins.

choices.label: Go along with it — it's common industry practice
choices.outcome: The drug harms patients outside the effective population. You bear partial responsibility.

choices.label: Request a legal review before publication
choices.outcome: Protective move. Legal review upholds full disclosure requirements.

rounds.coaching_moment: Publication bias is one of the most dangerous forms of scientific misconduct. The pressure to publish positive results corrupts the entire knowledge system.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Correlation Trap
rounds.scenario: Marketing wants to claim your product 'reduces stress by 40%' based on a survey. The survey had no control group. Do you approve the claim?

choices.label: No — without a control group, you can't claim causation
choices.outcome: Marketing is frustrated but respects your scientific reasoning. Claim is revised to 'users report...'

choices.label: Yes — surveys are valid evidence
choices.outcome: Claim goes live. A journalist runs their own test. You get a public correction.

choices.label: Yes, if they add a footnote about methodology
choices.outcome: The footnote is ignored. The misleading headline drives sales initially, then backfires.

rounds.coaching_moment: Correlation is not causation — and this distinction protects your integrity, your brand, and your customers.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Community Belief vs. Data
rounds.scenario: Your data shows a traditional farming practice reduces yields by 20%. The community has practiced it for generations. How do you present your findings?

choices.label: Present data, acknowledge tradition, and ask for dialogue
choices.outcome: Community engages. They trial a hybrid approach. Trust preserved.

choices.label: Present data only — facts should speak for themselves
choices.outcome: Community feels dismissed. They reject your findings entirely.

choices.label: Suppress data to avoid conflict
choices.outcome: Yields continue to decline. When truth comes out, trust is completely broken.

rounds.coaching_moment: Science and culture aren't opposites. The most effective change happens when data is presented with cultural humility.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Your Own Bias
rounds.scenario: You realize the hypothesis you've been testing for 2 years is probably wrong. You've invested heavily — colleagues are expecting positive results.

choices.label: Publish null results — negative findings matter for science
choices.outcome: Rare but brave. Others cite your paper to avoid the same dead end.

choices.label: Keep testing — maybe with more data it'll work out
choices.outcome: 18 more months pass. Same result. Sunk cost bias wins. You've wasted time that could have been spent on better questions.

choices.label: Reframe the research as exploratory rather than confirmatory
choices.outcome: Honest pivot. You extract useful learnings from an inconclusive study.

rounds.coaching_moment: Sunk cost fallacy is one of the hardest cognitive biases to overcome. The most scientific thing you can do is update your beliefs when the evidence changes — even when it's your own beliefs at stake.

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Teaching Critical Thinking
rounds.scenario: You're asked to design a school program on science literacy. What's the core skill you prioritize?

choices.label: How to evaluate sources and identify bias
choices.outcome: Students become information-literate. Applicable across every subject and life decision.

choices.label: Memorization of key scientific facts
choices.outcome: Strong foundation but limited transferability. Students struggle when facts are contested.

choices.label: How to design a simple experiment
choices.outcome: Excellent hands-on skill, but narrow without critical evaluation skills to interpret results.

rounds.coaching_moment: The meta-skill of evaluating evidence is more valuable than any specific piece of knowledge. Teach people how to think, not just what to think.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Disagreeing with Experts
rounds.scenario: A widely cited expert in your field holds a view contradicted by newer evidence you've read. You're presenting at a conference. Do you challenge them?

choices.label: Yes — present your evidence professionally and invite discussion
choices.outcome: Science progresses through challenge. The expert respects your rigor even if they disagree.

choices.label: No — defer to authority, you might be wrong
choices.outcome: The old view persists longer than necessary. Other attendees had similar doubts but also stayed quiet.

choices.label: Mention it in a footnote but don't make it a centerpiece
choices.outcome: Cautious but not fully honest. The evidence deserves a platform.

rounds.coaching_moment: Expertise deserves respect, not deference. Science advances when people are willing to respectfully challenge authority with evidence.

expert_pick.reason: Resilience research shows that processing setbacks openly builds stronger teams.

rounds.title: Your Legacy
rounds.scenario: Looking back on your career in science and society, what do you most want to be remembered for?

choices.label: Advancing knowledge, even when it was uncomfortable
choices.outcome: Your career is defined by courage. Others cite your integrity as inspiration.

choices.label: Building bridges between scientists and communities
choices.outcome: Your work has broad social impact. Knowledge reached people who needed it.

choices.label: Challenging the status quo and winning some, losing some
choices.outcome: Authentic record. Your failures taught others as much as your successes.

rounds.coaching_moment: The most important scientific contribution isn't a single discovery — it's a lifetime of intellectual honesty and courage.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

reflection_prompt: Which scenario in Science & Society was hardest for you to answer correctly? What belief did it challenge?
learning_objectives: Develop critical thinking through rounds gameplay
Build self-awareness about your strengths and areas for growth

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Science & Society: Truth Under Pressure Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of Science & Society: Truth Under Pressure. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.
